frameworks.name: Drop-Servicing via Google Business Profile
frameworks.definition: A zero-capital local-service arbitrage model: rank a Google Business Profile for a high-demand local service, accept inbound calls, subcontract jobs to independent contractors at their rate, and collect a 30-40% markup from the customer.

frameworks.name: GMB Ranking Stack
frameworks.definition: Three-element sequence for topping Google Maps results: (1) keyword-match business name, (2) review count matching top-3 incumbents, (3) fully SEO-optimized profile sections written by ChatGPT.

frameworks.name: Inspection-Commit Close
frameworks.definition: Instead of quoting over the phone, charge a small inspection fee ($60) that is waived if the customer proceeds; once a prospect pays the inspection fee they almost always proceed, because abandoning wastes their sunk commitment.

Google Business Profile ranked in top-3 for target keyword

claims.mechanism: Subcontractor handles labor at their desired rate; host marks up the customer-facing price by 30-40% and pockets the spread without spending on ads or labor.

claims.text: For local-service drop-servicing, high-ticket, high-urgency, evergreen services (plumbing, HVAC, electrical) produce substantially higher margins than low-ticket services because a 30-40% markup on a $5,000 job yields $1,500-2,000 whereas the same markup on a $200 job yields only $60-80.

conditions: Drop-servicing model with fixed 30-40% markup
Local trades market
claims.mechanism: Markup percentage is fixed; absolute dollar margin scales linearly with job ticket size, so high-ticket services disproportionately reward the same operational effort.

claims.text: A Google Maps market is worth entering for local-service drop-servicing when the target keyword has at least 400 monthly searches AND at least two of the top-three ranked businesses have fewer than 100 reviews; below 400 searches the call volume is insufficient to generate daily leads.
claims.speaker: anonymous host of weird_80k_biz_model.txt
conditions: Local-service drop-servicing business
Lead generation via Google Maps / Google Business Profile
claims.mechanism: Search volume determines the lead pool size; review count of incumbents determines the effort required to outrank them. Crossing both thresholds means enough demand exists and the barrier to ranking is achievable.

numbers.axis: monthly keyword search volume threshold for market entry

bounded_by: High-search markets also require proportionally more reviews to rank (200-300 vs 60)

claims.text: Ranking in the top position on Google Maps for a local-service keyword is primarily determined by two factors in sequence: (1) including the exact search keyword in the business profile name, and (2) matching or exceeding the review count of the top-ranked incumbent; SEO-optimized profile content is secondary.
claims.speaker: anonymous host of weird_80k_biz_model.txt
conditions: Google Maps / Google Business Profile ranking
Local-service keyword with moderate competition (top incumbents under 200 reviews)
claims.mechanism: Google's ranking algorithm favors exact keyword matches in business names over review count alone; a lower-review business with a keyword-matched name outranks a higher-review business with a generic name, as illustrated by the stucco Las Vegas example where 59-review 'Stucco Las Vegas' outranked 118-review competitors.
bounded_by: Does not apply to extremely competitive markets where many incumbents already have keyword-matched names and high review counts

claims.text: Refusing to give price quotes over the phone and instead charging a $60 inspection fee (waived if customer proceeds with the job) converts nearly 100% of callers who accept the inspection, because the $60 commitment creates sunk-cost anchoring that makes abandoning the process feel wasteful.

examples.text: The host ranked a plumbing Google Business Profile for a Canadian city starting in October 2025. Within two months (by December 2025), the profile was generating enough calls to produce ~$30,000 in net profit that month. Screenshots shown in the video include a $3,000 single day (December 29th) and multiple $400-$1,200 transaction records, all described as direct profit. The host contacted their first subcontractor plumber via Facebook in October 2025, offering to send inbound leads in exchange for a 40% margin on each job. That plumber later referred additional plumbers when he was too busy to take all jobs.

The host used stucco repair in Las Vegas as a live demonstration of the market-selection process. SEMrush keyword overview showed approximately 1,000 monthly searches for stucco-related terms in Las Vegas. The top-ranked Google Maps listing had 59 reviews (4.6 stars), outranking a competitor with 118 reviews (4.9 stars), because the lower-review business included both 'Stucco' and 'Las Vegas' in its name while the higher-review competitor did not. The host concluded that a new profile named 'Eric's Stucco Las Vegas' with 60 reviews and a 5-star average would rank first.

To accumulate reviews quickly, the host posted a Facebook Marketplace listing offering $25 gift cards for five Google reviews each. Additionally, the host recommends soliciting reviews from friends and family (targeting 10-20 reviews) and offering reciprocal reviews to other local businesses. ChatGPT is used to write review text containing relevant keywords (e.g., 'best plumbing company in San Diego, fixed my pipes'); the reviews are then posted from different Google accounts sourced through the methods above.

The host scripts the phone close as follows: when a customer asks for a price quote over the phone, the response is: 'Based on that issue, there could be a lot of different things causing the problem. What we always want to make sure is we're being super transparent with our pricing. So what we would typically do is have one of our technicians come out and assess the issue — that way they'll be able to see exactly what's causing it, give you a price, and we can get it done on the spot if you want to move forward. It's going to be $60 for the inspection, but if you do want to go ahead with it, we'll totally waive that and just charge you for the service itself.' Customers who accept the inspection convert at nearly 100% because they have already committed $60.

practices.text: Name your Google Business Profile to exactly match the primary search keyword for your service and city (e.g., 'Stucco Repair Las Vegas' or 'Plumbing San Diego') rather than using a branded or generic name.
Use SEMrush's keyword overview tool to verify at least 400 monthly searches for your target service keyword in your chosen area before investing time in a Google Business Profile there.
Fill every editable section of the Google Business Profile (description, products, services, posts) with ChatGPT-generated SEO-optimized copy that includes city and service keywords.
Reach out to potential subcontractors by telling them you 'run ads' for leads, not that you rank Google profiles, to avoid contractors understanding the full margin structure and renegotiating.
When expanding to multiple geographic profiles, buy a dedicated phone number for each profile (~$50/month total for several numbers) to keep lead streams separate and trackable.
Have the subcontractor text you their daily schedule each morning so you can book inspection appointments against their availability without double-booking.

Use Square or Stripe to take customer payment directly at job completion (send a link after the job is done) rather than letting the contractor collect; if cash payment is required, have the contractor collect and verify the amount by calling the customer afterward.
Agree on the markup percentage (30-40%) with the subcontractor before the first job to eliminate confusion and negotiation on a per-job basis.
